claims.value: Höpfner: Major Benekendorf, the commandant, wrote to the King that the citadel was secure against a coup de main and that, failing other orders, he would leave the enemy only the ruins of the fortress. The commandant's reply to the summons made to him, a copy of which went with Lannes's letter, was that the fortress would not surrender but would not oppose the passage of the French troops entering by the Potsdam gate and leaving by the Charlottenburg gate, provided they did not approach the fortress, its bridges and its gates. In Höpfner's account the commandant called a council of war in which all the members but the engineer captain Meinert voted to surrender, though no shot had yet been fired, citing the bad state of the works, the insufficient ammunition and garrison and the harm a defence would do to the King's interest and the inhabitants'. He declared to the parlementaire his readiness to surrender, the judge-advocate was to draw up the points of capitulation, and during this work he is said to have waved his handkerchief to the post at the drawbridge to let it down. He was later sentenced to be shot, and pardoned by the King to fortress imprisonment for life. Bertrand reported that a young officer said only that they had the King's order to defend themselves and would die, and that the commandant is old.

claims.value: Bodart records the capitulation of Spandau on 25 October: the garrison surrendered without a fight to the French under Lannes. The capitulation, signed at Spandau on 25 October by General Victor for Lannes and by Major Benekendorff, let the officers go where they wished with their arms and effects, had Lannes undertake to ask the Emperor that the invalids and their wives keep their effects and stay in the citadel, made the NCOs and soldiers prisoners of war and handed over the fortress at once with its artillery, arms, munitions and supplies. Höpfner says French soldiers occupied the walls before the capitulation was concluded, leaving the garrison at the enemy's mercy, but the French granted the terms already offered.

The officers of the garrison of Spandau will withdraw where they wish with their arms, clothes and other effects belonging to them'; 'art. 2. claims.value: Side B held the citadel of Spandau, a permanent fortress that Lannes describes as standing in the middle of a lake and capable of a great defence. Höpfner says the citadel was in no particular state but had no practicable breach, nor could one easily be made, because its rampart consisted of several tiers of vaults; even an enemy who approached it and seized the covered way could not cross the main ditch except under the fire of the works; but for want of time the parapets could not be raised, and gabions had to be made instead. Bertrand reported an enclosure with a parapet and about a dozen guns in battery around the fort, which seemed to him crowded with buildings and easy to set on fire.
claims.rationale: Coded B_fortified: the citadel's works were permanent and held by side B, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'only on the 23rd did workers arrive from the country, who were now used to repair the citadel. It was in no particular condition, but there was also no practicable breach, nor could one easily be made, as the rampart consisted of several vaults lying one above the other'; 'but even if the enemy approached the citadel by means of it and seized the covered way, he was still not able to cross the main ditch except under the fire of the works' (OCR); 'it was just as disadvantageous that, likewise for want of time, no work could be done on raising the parapets; gabions had to be made instead' (OCR); Bertrand, as in claim side-b-strength-french for the heading and signature and in claim side-a-information for the enclosure (OCR); 'around the fort a dozen guns in battery' (OCR); 'the fort seems to me crowded with buildings and easy to set on fire' (OCR); Lannes, as in claim side-b-strength-french for the heading and date and in claim spandau-ground for the lake.

open_questions: Deferred: Lannes's promised return of what was found in the place; Bertrand's sketch and the plan of the attack; the records of the Prussian judicial inquiries held after the war, on which by the preface of his first volume Höpfner's work chiefly rests, and of the commandant's trial. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated: the guns ordered from Berlin (Höpfner, p. 128), the hours and dates of the summonses and of the council (pp. 130-131), the number of the light infantry regiment (p. 130), the patrol's horses (p. 130), the year of the sentence (p. 131), the widths of the water in Bertrand's first report (Foucart t. II, pp. 315-316), and the cartridges ordered in Höpfner's footnote (p. 129).

Most consequential gap: the garrison's size, given as not over 900 (Höpfner), 1,000 (Bodart) and 1,200 (Lannes, and the Emperor's prisoners), with Bertrand's informants' 800, or 1,400 with the 600 more that apparently were there (our arithmetic), and his own sight of no more than 400; Lannes's promised return of the place or a French list of the prisoners could settle it. The guns are similarly uncertain (71 in Höpfner's ammunition count, 80 in the Emperor's letter, 50 to 90 by Bertrand's informants).

Disputes kept as separate claims: the garrison (not over 900, Höpfner; 1,000, Bodart; 1,200, Lannes and the Emperor; Bertrand's estimates); the guns (71 in Höpfner's ammunition count; 80, the Emperor; 50, 60 or 90, Bertrand's informants; a dozen in battery reported by Bertrand, OCR); whether the capitulation was concluded before the French occupied the walls (Höpfner says not).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked); Foucart, t. II (the French side's documents: Latour-Maubourg's note, Bertrand's reports, Lannes's letter with the capitulation and the commandant's reply, the Emperor's letter to Davout); Höpfner, Bd. 2, 2nd edition (the Prussian side's history; by the preface of his first volume the work rests chiefly on the records of the judicial inquiries held after the war into those who fell into captivity by capitulation or otherwise, but the Spandau passage does not name its sources).
